articles.title: Homem dá golpes de enxada na cabeça da enteada e foge em Itapemirim | G1
articles.standfirst: Os policiais fizeram buscas na casa, no quintal e nas proximidades, mas não encontraram o suspeito. A vítima foi socorrida e levada a um hospital por vizinhos.
articles.summary: Os policiais fizeram buscas na casa, no quintal e nas proximidades, mas não encontraram o suspeito. A vítima foi socorrida e levada a um hospital por vizinhos.
articles.body:
Homem dá golpes de enxada na cabeça da enteada e foge em Itapemirim, no Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação

Uma mulher de 23 anos foi atingida por golpes de enxada na cabeça pelo próprio padrasto, de 63 anos, na localidade de Ilha do Gato, em Itapemirim, no Sul do Espírito Santo, neste domingo (15). Segundo a Polícia Militar, o suspeito fugiu logo após o ocorrido e não foi localizado.

A vítima foi socorrida por duas pessoas em estado grave e levada ao Hospital Evangélico Litoral Sul em um veículo particular. Depois, encaminhada à Santa Casa. Familiares não souberam informar o motivo da agressão.

Os policiais foram acionados para atender a uma denúncia de tentativa de homicídio. Ao chegarem ao endereço, não encontraram a vítima nem o suspeito.

Na residência onde teria ocorrido a agressão, os militares encontraram uma enxada ensanguentada, além de marcas de sangue espalhadas pelo chão e na varanda do imóvel.

Os policiais fizeram buscas na casa, no quintal e nas proximidades, mas não encontraram o suspeito. Outras equipes também realizaram patrulhamento na região, sem sucesso.

A vítima não morava na residência. Segundo parentes, a mãe dela e o suspeito eram separados, mas viviam na mesma residência.

Ainda de acordo com relato de um familiar, o homem dava em cima da jovem, mas ela não correspondia. Neste domingo, ele tentou olhar ela tomando banho. Isso foi o motivo de uma discussão.

A mãe dela tentou separar os dois. Na briga, a jovem foi jogada contra o muro e caiu. Nesse momento que ele deu os golpes de enxada na cabeça dela.

A mulher sofreu uma lesão no lado direito da cabeça e teve uma hemorragia. Ela chegou ao hospital em estado gravíssimo e precisou de ventilação mecânica.

O g1 não conseguiu atualizar o estado da saúde da mulher, mas ela estava internada no pronto-socorro da Santa Casa até a última atualização da reportagem.

"Nos deparamos com bastante sangue. Familiares falaram que o suspeito tinha efetuado os golpes. Não informaram a possível motivação. Os médicos disseram que o estado dela é gavíssimo e aguardam transferência para Vitória. Perdeu muito sangue. O essencial foi o socorro imediato", disse o sargento Ernane, da Polícia Militar.

A Polícia Militar encaminhou o caso à Delegacia de Polícia Judiciária de Itapemirim.

A Polícia Civil informou que o caso seguirá sob investigação da Delegacia Regional de Itapemirim e até a publicação da reportagem, nenhum suspeito também foi detido. Informações podem ser repassadas de forma sigilosa ao Disque-Denúncia 181, no site disquedenuncia181.es.gov.br/ ou no WhatsApp (27) 99253-8181.

articles.title: Estudantes em tratamento fazem Enem em hospital e sonham com faculdade | G1
articles.standfirst: Julia Faria, de 19 anos, e amiga Nathalia Portilho, de 17, fazem o exame no Centro Boldrini, em Campinas. Aplicação em ambiente hospitalar é prevista pelo MEC.
articles.summary: 4. Aplicação em ambiente hospitalar é prevista pelo MEC para candidatos internados ou que precisam de isolamento por motivos de saúde.
articles.body:
As amigas Julia Faria , de 19 anos, e Nathalia Portilho , de 17, farão o segundo dia do Enem , neste domingo (15), em salas individuais no Centro Boldrini, hospital de Campinas (SP) referência no tratamento de câncer infantil.

Ambas passam por tratamento no hospital e também fizeram o primeiro dia de prova dentro da unidade, onde conciliam os cuidados médicos com o sonho de ingressar na universidade .

Natural de Niterói (RJ), Julia se mudou na infância para Campinas . Aos 7 anos, descobriu um mielodisplasia , um tipo de câncer da medula óssea e do sangue, e iniciou o tratamento no Boldrini.

Aos 7 anos, Julia descobriu um mielodisplasia, um tipo de câncer da medula óssea e do sangue — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O sonho da jovem é conseguir, por meio do Enem, chegar ao curso de medicina. “Eu quero muito ser médica. Eu acho que eu tenho esse sonho desde pequenininha mesmo, por viver por viver, ver muita gente nessa luta diária, no tratamento contra o câncer", disse.

"E eu falei que eu quero fazer a diferença, eu quero estar meio que na área da pesquisa, eu quero achar cura pra doenças, mas ao mesmo tempo eu quero estar ali naquela terapia intensiva, em UTIs, em emergências, aonde precisar", explica.

✍🏻 O Ministério da Educação (MEC) permite a aplicação do Enem em hospitais para estudantes internados ou que precisam de isolamento por motivos de saúde. Para isso, é necessário solicitar o atendimento em classe hospitalar durante a inscrição, apresentar laudo médico e declaração do hospital sobre as condições para realizar a prova.

Julia Faria durante a preparação para o vestibular — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

É a segunda vez que Julia presta o Enem. Na primeira, ficou preocupada com relatos sobre a rigidez da aplicação. "E eu estava com muito medo, porque, pelo que já me falaram sobre o Enem, falaram que os fiscais eram bravos, que é muita pressão, e eu falei: 'Gente, vai dar ruim'", lembra.

A experiência, porém, foi positiva. Segundo a estudante, o apoio recebido durante a aplicação no hospital ajudou a reduzir a ansiedade . Neste ano, ela viajou do Rio de Janeiro para Campinas especialmente para realizar a prova.

"Eu cheguei domingo de manhã, eu vim para a casa de apoio, coloquei minhas malas, dei uma estudada com a outra paciente que também fez, a Natália, e nós fomos juntas", comentou.

Durante a prova, Julia precisa seguir horários específicos para tomar medicamentos . Os fiscais acompanham sua rotina e oferecem apoio sempre que necessário. "O atendimento é mais carinhoso porque eu tenho que tomar remédios. Eles me avisam os meus horários, sempre perguntam se está tudo bem e se eu estou com alguma dor."

Júlia, à direita, e Natália, à esquerda — Foto: Reprodção/Redes Sociais

Já Nathália, natural de Palmas (TO), está em tratamento desde março de 2025, quando descobriu a Leucemia Linfoblástica Aguda da célula T (LLA-T) . Passou por um transplante de medula em Jaú (SP) há 10 meses e hoje faz acompanhamento nos dois hospitais.

Mais nova que a amiga, Nathália está na fase de refletir sobre a futura profissão. "Há diversas áreas que me atraem, porém estou pesquisando e descobrindo sobre elas".

Ela participa do Enem pela primeira vez e, no primeiro domingo, acordou tranquila no dia do exame. "Ao abrir a prova, minha maior preocupação era quanto ao gerenciamento de tempo de execução da prova, mas depois fui me recompondo", comenta Nathalia.

A estudante relata que a experiência foi marcante por ser sua primeira participação no Enem e por realizar a prova dentro de um ambiente hospitalar. Segundo Nathalia, a possibilidade de fazer o exame em um local seguro foi importante devido às restrições impostas pelo tratamento.

🏥 As estudantes não são pacientes internadas no hospital , mas recorreram à aplicação em classe hospitalar porque, devido às condições de saúde, precisam de ambiente controlado e seguro.

Julia durante sua preparação para o vestibular — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O desafio de conciliar estudo e tratamento

Para se preparar para o Enem, Julia estudou em um cursinho on-line e contou com a ajuda de um professor da cidade onde mora. "Ele [professor] tem um método, um repertório. Porque ele já é médico e eu quero ser médica, e ele literalmente me ajudou bastante nesse processo também".

Nos períodos de internação, ela afirma que nem sempre conseguiu manter os estudos, mas avalia que teve um bom desempenho ao longo do ano. Conciliar o tratamento com a preparação para o exame foi um dos principais desafios.

"É muito complicado, né? Porque o Enem abre as portas para o nosso futuro. Mas, muitas das vezes, quando a gente está fazendo um tratamento, a gente pensa que aquilo dali é só aquilo dali que a gente tem que focar", explica.

Julia também destacou o apoio pedagógico oferecido pelo Hospital Boldrini. "Porque, quando eu falava que eu não queria, elas iam no quarto, sempre me dando uma atividade, sempre conversando comigo", comenta a estudante

"Quando eu falava que eu não aguentava, até mesmo a questão de fazer alguma atividade, eu sempre tive muita afta. Como eu tenho imunidade baixa, eu ficava com dor para falar, e elas falavam: 'Júlia, não precisa falar nada, a gente só vai te explicar'", contou.

Além do acompanhamento pedagógico, o hospital mantém uma biblioteca e ações voltadas ao incentivo educacional . "Eles sempre mostram uma forma estratégica para a gente continuar sendo incentivada a estudar, mesmo passando por tudo que a gente passa. Eu acho isso muito importante."

Nathalia Portilho, de 17 anos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Nathalia afirma que sua principal base para a prova foi o conhecimento adquirido durante o ensino fundamental e médio. Segundo ela, não houve estudo aprofundado de conteúdos, mas sim preparação voltada à estrutura do exame.

"Estudei apenas a estrutura da prova, como funciona cada dia, e estratégias para a prova, mas, quanto a conteúdo, até mesmo devido ao tempo, organização e tratamento, acabei não dando muita exclusividade para estudo", conta.

Ela conta também que já havia praticado redações anteriormente, mas que o formato do Enem era novidade por ser sua primeira participação. A jovem comenta que sua família é um grande apoio nesse processo, tanto emocional quanto para acesso a conhecimentos juntos, já que sua irmã também realizou a prova pela primeira vez.

A jovem afirma que nem sempre é fácil estudar durante o tratamento. "Conciliar o estudo com o tratamento é difícil devido a várias questões, como a falta de uma rotina fixa, que em muitos casos limita nosso tempo, e variações de estado de disposição. Há dias em que simplesmente não estamos bem e só queremos ficar quietos."

Hospital do Centro Infantil Boldrini, localizado em Campinas (SP) — Foto: Ely Venâncio/EPTV

Julia afirma que as próprias pedagogas do hospital orientam os pacientes a realizarem a inscrição para o Enem com o acompanhamento da equipe.

A medida permite que o Boldrini comunique ao Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep) a necessidade de apoio especial durante a aplicação das provas.

"Porque nós comunicamos que a gente precisa desse suporte e elas comunicam o Inep, que podem dar esse suporte. A gente manda a nossa inscrição e elas mandam a nossa inscrição também com o nosso nome, informando que o Boldrini está disposto a ajudar," explica.

Provas Enem 2026. — Foto: Bruna Araújo/MEC

De acordo com a pedagoga do Boldrini Cibelle Bittencourt, o edital do Enem publicado pelo Inep prevê a possibilidade de aplicação em ambiente hospitalar. Para pedi o serviço, o estudante deve apresentar um relatório médico durante a inscrição e pedir atendimento em classe hospitalar.

Bittencourt afirma que alguns pacientes conseguem estudar sozinhos, mas outros precisam de acompanhamento durante a preparação. Nesses casos, o hospital oferece apoio pedagógico e conta com voluntários que ajudam nos estudos, o que permite que os jovens mantenham os projetos educacionais durante o tratamento.

"O que é bacana para eles que estão fazendo o tratamento é que eles vão ter essa oportunidade, poderiam perder esse ano, então eles vão ter essa oportunidade".

"Eles ficam numa sala, geralmente só o paciente e o fiscal, não fica numa sala com 30, 40 pessoas, porque podem correr o risco, às vezes estão com a imunidade baixa, podem correr o risco de pegar alguma coisa".

Ela afirma que a oportunidade é fundamental para que adolescentes e jovens em tratamento mantenham seus planos de ingresso no ensino superior e não precisem interromper seus projetos profissionais.

"Aplicar o Enem no hospital vai muito mais do que um direito do paciente. É uma perspectiva de futuro, de continuidade da vida e dos sonhos."

Nathalia em seu tempo de lazer — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Julia diz que procura incentivar outros jovens em tratamento a não abandonarem os estudos nem o sonho de ingressar na universidade . Segundo ela, o apoio entre os pacientes faz diferença durante a preparação para o Enem e outros vestibulares.

"Pode ter certeza que eu estou ali para ajudar. Eu e a Natália já fizemos muitas aulas juntas. Quando uma não estava animada, a outra ajudava. Então eu falo que eles têm que ter amigos ali dentro do hospital que reforcem isso, que é só uma fase, que tudo vai passar."

Julia finaliza agradecendo o trabalho das pedagogas do hospital, que considera fundamentais para sua trajetória educacional. "Elas foram algumas das melhores amigas que eu tive nesse processo e me incentivaram a continuar estudando."

"Encarem como se fosse apenas mais um simulado e mantenham a calma, não se desesperem, porque essa prova não define de fato o conhecimento que você adquiriu em sala de aula, mas requer uma interpretação e compreensão do todo, e sempre haverá novas oportunidades", conclui Nátalia.

articles.title: Estudante em tratamento contra tumor cerebral lança dois livros e inspira colegas em MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Aos 16 anos, Júlio Emanuel de Almeida encontra na literatura uma forma de enfrentar a doença e apresenta os livros O Sétimo Filho da Lua e A Lua de Sangue.
articles.summary: Aos 16 anos, Júlio Emanuel de Almeida encontra na literatura uma forma de enfrentar a doença e apresenta os livros O Sétimo Filho da Lua e A Lua de Sangue.
articles.body:
O estudante Júlio Emanuel de Almeida, de 16 anos, lançou nesta semana dois livros em Carmo do Rio Claro , no Sul de Minas. Paciente em tratamento contra um tumor cerebral, ele encontrou na escrita uma forma de enfrentar a doença e transformar a imaginação em histórias.

Entre páginas que misturam dramas e lendas brasileiras, o jovem escritor compartilha um universo criado por ele. O interesse pelos livros começou ainda na infância.

"Desde pequeno assim, sempre gostei de ler, sempre fui na biblioteca, escrever, tipo escrever no caderno, fazer caça-palavra", contou o estudante.

Estudante em tratamento contra tumor cerebral lança dois livros e inspira colegas em MG — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

Júlio mergulhou no mundo da leitura quando tinha apenas quatro anos. O sonho de se tornar escritor surgiu mais tarde e foi realizado no ano passado. As histórias de fantasia estão entre suas principais inspirações.

Agora, ele lança os livros O Sétimo Filho da Lua e sua continuação, A Lua de Sangue. Para o futuro, o jovem já planeja escrever uma autobiografia.

"O que ajuda mesmo na escrita é principalmente a imaginação. Você deita a cabeça no travesseiro, pensa, fecha o olho, deixa a imaginação escrever por cima. Aí isso ajuda bastante, pensar, imaginar como é que vai ser e escrever", afirmou.

O incentivo à leitura veio de dentro de casa. A mãe, Ana Paula Borges de Almeida Barbosa, conta que sempre teve o hábito de ler e procurou transmitir esse costume aos filhos.

"Eu sempre gostei, eu sempre fui muito entusiasta do livro, então desde pequeno lá em casa os presentes eram livro, era livro de ilustração e foi indo. Desde meu primeiro menino até agora o Júlio principalmente, a gente introduziu a literatura desde pequeno", disse.

Em 2024, Júlio recebeu o diagnóstico de um tumor cerebral e iniciou tratamento no Hospital Regional do Câncer de Passos. Segundo a mãe, o quadro apresentou melhora.

"A gente está vivendo um dia após o outro agora, mas ele graças a Deus, eu não sei se a gente tem tanto crédito com Deus, mas ele melhorou. Ele está melhorando, o tumor paralisou, ele está vivendo o dia a dia dele normal, tem as amizades dele, tem os amiguinhos dele, ele vem para a escola", relatou Ana Paula.

A Escola Monsenhor Mário Araújo Guimarães, em Carmo do Rio Claro, apoiou o estudante durante o processo de publicação das obras.

"A gente tem que entender o aluno como um todo. Ele é um universo como um todo e esse universo tem que ser respeitado, tem que ser explorado. E quando a gente começa a explorar as potencialidades de cada um, acontece isso", afirmou o professor Júnio César Oliveira Martins.

Entre os amigos, a expectativa para os lançamentos também é grande. Eles destacam a determinação e o otimismo do estudante.

"Apesar de todas as dificuldades que ele passa, ele sempre foi um menino muito alegre, otimista, sempre buscou atrás de seus sonhos e a gente tem muito orgulho dele", disse o estudante Miguel Silva Garcia.

"Olha, é uma experiência única ter o Júlio nas nossas vidas e é uma experiência única, porque quase ninguém tem um amigo escritor e o Júlio é uma pessoa incrível. Então, sim, ele é uma ótima pessoa e eu tenho muito orgulho dele", afirmou a estudante Amanda Santana Guilherme.

Para Júlio, manter uma atitude positiva durante o tratamento tem sido fundamental tanto para a saúde quanto para a produção literária.

"Enfrentando essa doença que eu tenho, existe muito otimismo ao invés do pessimismo. Porque o pessimismo tende a piorar, segundo o especialista lá do hospital onde eu faço tratamento. Aí, quando eles falam que o Júlio é muito alegre, muito contente, eu me sinto melhor e acho que eu vou melhorar cada vez mais rápido. Isso ajudou bastante, muito mais na escrita do livro e principalmente nesse grande evento de lançamento desse livro que vai ser hoje. Muito ansioso, animado, vou treinar os discursos que vou falar e principalmente o autógrafo", contou o estudante.

articles.title: Vídeo: motorista atropela homem em São Caetano, na Grande SP; vítima teve compressão na medula | G1
articles.standfirst: Condutor do veículo tentou fugir, mas foi contido por populares.
articles.summary: Condutor do veículo tentou fugir, mas foi contido por populares.
articles.body:
Um motorista, que dirigia por uma via em São Caetano do Sul , na Grande São Paulo , atropelou um homem na Rua Piauí, próximo ao número 653, na noite do último sábado (14).

No momento da ocorrência, a vítima de 26 anos, que se chama Henrique, andava com mais duas pessoas, sua cunhada e namorada, na calçada e em parte da via. Ele tentou proteger uma das mulheres segundos antes de ser atingido por trás pelo veículo. Henrique foi arremeçado para a lateral da calçada e apenas ele ficou ferido.

O nome do condutor do veículo é Pedro Giannini Nogueira Pires, de 34 anos, segundo informações da polícia civil. No momento que sucedeu a batida, ele se negou a fazer o teste do bafômetro. Testemunhas que estavam no local no momento do acidente informaram que ele tentou fugir, mas foi contido até a chegada das autoridades.

Motorista suspeito de dirigir embriagado atropela homem em São Caetano e tenta fugir, dizem testemunhas — Foto: Reprodução

Quando foi realizado o exame clínico, feito após o atropelamento, no entanto, o resultado foi negativo para embriaguez. Esse tipo de teste envolve, por exemplo, pedir ao indivíduo que ande em linha reta.

Henrique está internado no Hospital São Luiz de São Caetano com lesões na cabeça. Ele está consciente e estável do ponto de vista neurológico. No entanto, houve uma compressão na medula, impedindo que, por ora, ele consiga mexer a perna ou urinar.

A vítima será submetida a exames para confirmar se será necessária cirurgia devido ao inchaço da medula.

Segundo o advogado da vítima, o condutor não está preso. Ainda será instaurado um inquérito policial pra apurar as circunstâncias do ocorrido. A vítima será ouvida quando estiver nas condições adequadas.

O caso foi registrado na Delegacia de Polícia de São Caetano do Sul como lesão corporal culposa na direção de veículo automotor.

Pedro Giannini Nogueira Pires (à direita nas fotos), era o condutor do veículo que atropelou Henrique em São Caetano — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

articles.title: Hackers expõem dados de 22 milhões ligados aos Correios da França | G1
articles.standfirst: Vazamento atinge o equivalente a cerca de um terço da população francesa e está no centro de uma investigação judicial.
articles.summary: Vazamento atinge o equivalente a cerca de um terço da população francesa e está no centro de uma investigação judicial.
articles.body:
A cibersegurança continua sendo uma preocupação crescente. — Foto: Freepik

A La Poste, equivalente aos Correios no Brasil e um dos maiores grupos de serviços da França, confirmou no sábado (14) que sua subsidiária Maileva foi vítima de um ataque cibernético em setembro. Segundo a empresa, o vazamento de dados atingiu cerca de 22 milhões de pessoas e colocou a companhia no centro de uma investigação judicial.

O volume de informações expostas equivale a aproximadamente um terço da população francesa e faz do caso um dos maiores vazamentos de dados já registrados no país. O episódio amplia a preocupação com a segurança de dados em grandes organizações francesas.

A Maileva, empresa especializada no envio de correspondências profissionais para pequenas e médias empresas e para companhias de porte intermediário, é utilizada para o envio de holerites, cartas registradas, faturas, notificações administrativas e convocações de assembleias, entre outros documentos.

Segundo o grupo, a invasão ocorreu em meados de setembro e levou à exposição de informações de destinatários das empresas clientes da plataforma. Entre os dados vazados estão nome, sobrenome e endereço postal. A empresa afirma que dados bancários e outras informações financeiras não foram comprometidos.

A Maileva integra a Docaposte, braço de serviços digitais da La Poste. A plataforma declara ter mais de 70 mil usuários e ter processado 180 milhões de documentos em 2024.

A empresa informou ter comunicado o incidente à Comissão Nacional de Informática e Liberdades (CNIL), autoridade francesa responsável pela proteção de dados pessoais, e apresentado uma denúncia às autoridades. Segundo o grupo, uma investigação judicial está em andamento.

Por que a La Poste é tão importante na França

A repercussão do caso também está ligada à posição ocupada pela La Poste na vida cotidiana dos franceses. Embora seja mais conhecida por sua atividade postal, a companhia ampliou suas operações nas últimas décadas e se tornou um grande grupo de serviços.

Além da distribuição de cartas e encomendas em todo o território francês, a empresa atua nas áreas bancária, financeira, digital e de gestão documental.

Por meio de diversas subsidiárias, atende empresas, administrações públicas e milhões de cidadãos, o que ajuda a explicar a abrangência potencial de um incidente envolvendo sistemas utilizados para o envio de correspondências em larga escala.

As informações expostas pertencem a pessoas que receberam correspondências enviadas por empresas e instituições que utilizam os serviços da Maileva, e não apenas aos clientes diretos da plataforma.

Segundo informações divulgadas pelo site especializado Cyberattaque.org, entre os afetados estão destinatários de comunicações de empresas de habitação social, pacientes de laboratórios de análises clínicas e usuários de hospitais franceses. O portal cita, entre outros exemplos, correspondências enviadas por organizações de habitação social como Flandre Opale Habitat e Altéal, além de laboratórios ligados ao grupo Inovie, como Inovie AXBIO, BioMedilab e Biofusion.

Entre os casos mencionados também está o do Hospital Foch, localizado em Suresnes, nos arredores de Paris. De acordo com o site especializado, um invasor teria acessado o conteúdo de determinadas cartas de cobrança encaminhadas a pacientes.

Esses documentos continham informações adicionais, incluindo números de faturas, datas de atendimento e valores pendentes de pagamento. Segundo o portal, o acesso teria ocorrido por intermédio da empresa Kiwee.care, especializada na cobrança extrajudicial de dívidas médicas e que utiliza a Maileva para impressão e expedição de correspondências.

O Cyberattaque.org afirma ainda que outros estabelecimentos de saúde atendidos pela Kiwee.care, que trabalha com diversas organizações do setor de saúde francês, também podem ter sido atingidos pelo incidente. A Maileva afirma que todas as empresas envolvidas foram informadas sobre o ocorrido, em conformidade com a regulamentação francesa.

O caso se soma a uma sequência de ataques cibernéticos e vazamentos de dados que vêm atingindo grandes empresas e órgãos públicos franceses nos últimos anos. Em 2025, a própria La Poste foi alvo de um ataque reivindicado por hackers pró-Rússia poucos dias antes do Natal, período considerado o mais intenso para as operações do grupo.

Na semana passada, o banco Crédit Mutuel Arkéa informou ter sido alvo de um ataque cibernético cujo impacto financeiro foi estimado em cerca de € 100 milhões. Em 2024, os operadores de gestão de pagamentos de despesas médicas Almerys e Viamedis sofreram um vazamento que atingiu mais de 33 milhões de pessoas.

Também em 2024, a agência pública de emprego France Travail registrou uma invasão que resultou na exposição de dados de 36,8 milhões de usuários. Mais recentemente, ataques contra a administração tributária francesa levaram ao roubo de dados de aproximadamente 700 mil contribuintes.

Especialistas e relatórios sobre segurança digital apontam que a França figura entre os países mais atingidos por ataques cibernéticos na Europa. Entre os fatores apontados estão o peso da economia francesa, a ampla digitalização de empresas e serviços públicos e o papel desempenhado pelo país em temas internacionais, incluindo seu apoio à Ucrânia desde o início da guerra contra a Rússia.

Os números divulgados pela CNIL mostram uma tendência de alta dos vazamentos de dados. Em 2024, a França registrou mais de 5.600 violações de dados pessoais, um aumento de 20% em relação ao ano anterior.

O episódio envolvendo a Maileva reforça a preocupação das autoridades com a vulnerabilidade de grandes bases de dados e com os riscos associados à crescente interconexão entre empresas privadas, hospitais, bancos e serviços públicos.

*Com informações da agência de notícias France Presse.

articles.title: Ebola in DR Congo: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola.
articles.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
articles.body:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Recovery of Ebola patients offers rare moments of joy at epicentre of outbreak

articles.title: Millions of Americans use marijuana to sleep, but new study raises troubling questions
articles.summary: A Northwestern Medicine study found that marijuana users had objectively worse sleep quality, even though they didn't perceive their sleep as worse. Other experts weighed in.
articles.body: Marijuana may be making sleep quality worse, despite its widespread use as a sleep aid, a recent Northwestern Medicine study found. The findings of the study, which included 1,266 participants, showed that both lifetime and recent cannabis users objectively had worse sleep quality, although they did not report their sleep to be worse. Participants were monitored for almost 35 years, from young adulthood into middle age, with scientists tracking their use of cannabis over time. AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING In middle age, participants wore a sleep monitor on their wrist for a week and filled out surveys about their sleep quality. This allowed researchers to compare objective and subjective reports of participants’ sleep. "Our data do not support the belief that cannabis is helpful as a sleep aid," said senior study author Mercedes R. Carnethon, Ph.D., as Northwestern Now reported. "As cannabis becomes increasingly available and accepted, it's important to better understand its long-term associations with health behaviors such as sleep," Carnethon added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Among all participants, a greater lifetime exposure to marijuana was linked to worse objective sleep quality. Those who had a higher cannabis usage over time were generally asleep for a lower percentage of the night and experienced more sleep disruption. Similarly, recent cannabis users were more likely to have more sleep fragmentation and lower sleep efficiency, compared to people who never used the substance. The study also found there was a much higher chance that recent cannabis users would sleep longer than eight hours per night. The study discusses the differences between objective and subjective reports of sleep quality. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "What makes this study particularly interesting is that participants who used cannabis demonstrated objectively poorer sleep, yet their own assessments of sleep quality did not reflect those differences," Alfred Joshua, M.D., a board-certified emergency medicine physician based in California, told Fox News Digital. (He was not involved with the new study.) "In other words, someone may believe marijuana is helping them sleep, while objective measurements suggest otherwise." Researchers considered multiple outside factors including age, race, sex, smoking frequency, alcohol consumption, physical activity and more. Even with these factors taken into account, the study found a consistent correlation between cannabis use and poorer objectively measured sleep. The mode of cannabis consumption, such as smoking versus taking edibles, was not considered. "These findings raise important questions." "It is not surprising that the actual quality of sleep of these subjects, after chronic marijuana use, is poor compared to those who do not smoke marijuana because people who claim that they need to smoke marijuana before they go to sleep, in order to relax, are only kidding themselves," board-certified psychiatrist Carole Lieberman, M.D., of California told Fox News Digital. (She, too, was not affiliated with the new study.) "It is more a psychological addiction than a physical one," she added. "They enjoy the high that they get right away, but the marijuana doesn't help them to sleep better." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The researchers found that greater cumulative cannabis exposure was associated with reduced sleep efficiency, increased sleep fragmentation and more time spent awake after initially falling asleep," said Joshua, the board-certified emergency medicine physician. "These findings raise important questions about whether habitual marijuana use is a sustainable strategy for managing sleep problems," he added. Fox News Digital recently reported on other cannabis findings. A study of nearly 450,000 American adults, for instance, linked cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The findings were scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9. They showed that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users. Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

articles.title: Zimbabwe’s HIV gains face a test among young people
articles.summary: New prevention tools offer hope, but reaching young people remains a challenge.
articles.body:
Harare, Zimbabwe – When Shaun Moyo started nursing at Parirenyatwa Hospital in Harare in the late 1990s, the effects of the HIV epidemic were visible in the hospital wards and beyond them. Patients filled the wards, she recalls, while funerals had become a familiar part of everyday life.

Nearly three decades later, the picture has changed. Antiretroviral treatment has transformed the lives of people living with HIV. Condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and other prevention options also give young people more ways to protect themselves.

But Moyo, now a 48-year-old nurse working locum shifts at two major public hospitals in Harare, worries that some young people may not fully appreciate the risks.

Her concern reflects a wider challenge for Zimbabwe: how to protect hard-won progress against HIV while ensuring that young people understand, can access and are willing to use the prevention tools available to them.

Dr Misheck Ruwende, a Zimbabwean family physician and advocate for reducing HIV stigma, shares that concern. In a public address on Twitter in September, followed online by Al Jazeera, members of the public and other local journalists, Ruwende warned that the country risked losing some of the gains made over decades.

“The sad part is that this is coming at a time we have the best options to prevent HIV, from rapid testing, PrEP, condoms, PEP to injectables,” Ruwende said.

“It wasn’t like that in the late 90s to early 2000s. It looks like we are now reversing all this huge success we had notched in recent times,” he added.

The scale of Zimbabwe’s progress is clear in the national figures. UNAIDS estimates that annual new HIV infections fell from 79,000 in 2010 to 15,000 in 2023. Among people aged 15 to 24, infections declined from an estimated 27,000 to 4,400 over the same period.

But falling infections do not mean the threat has disappeared. The challenge is to sustain those gains among young people navigating relationships, economic pressures and uneven access to youth-friendly health services. It is a challenge shared across a region that continues to carry a heavy burden of HIV.

A generation that has forgotten the fear

For Moyo, the contrast between the epidemic she witnessed as a young nurse and the attitudes she encounters today can be difficult to accept.

“Seeing today’s youth who are blessed with condoms, ARVs and PrEP meds makes me furious,” she said. “In the 90s every weekend was a trek to cemeteries, not weddings.”

She believes the availability of effective treatment has changed how some young people perceive HIV. Because the virus is no longer the immediate death sentence it was once widely understood to be, she worries that some underestimate the consequences of infection.

Moyo recalled conversations involving her son and his friends on Facebook, where one comment suggested that “getting blood pressure is worse than HIV”.

Her observations are personal, not scientific evidence of changing attitudes among young people. But they point to a difficult public health task: explaining why prevention remains important even though treatment has made HIV a manageable chronic condition for many.

The concern is not confined to Zimbabwe. UNAIDS estimated that 210,000 adolescent girls and young women aged 15 to 24 acquired HIV worldwide in 2023. Some 160,000 of those infections were in sub-Saharan Africa, while nearly 60 percent of the global total occurred in Eastern and Southern Africa.

South Africa, Zimbabwe’s neighbour, illustrates the continuing scale of the epidemic in the region. UNAIDS estimated that 7.7 million people were living with HIV there in 2023.

Data from Gauteng province also point to concerns about sexually transmitted infections. Between April and December 2023, 167,109 males attended public health facilities in the province, and 67,400 were treated for Male Urethritis Syndrome (MUS), which is associated with sexually transmitted infections. The provincial health department reported that MUS incidence increased from 12 percent in 2020 to 15 percent in 2023. The condition is not itself a measure of HIV infections.

For Dr Linda-Gail Bekker, a South African HIV physician-scientist and co-author of the report on the PURPOSE 1 clinical trial, the response must combine scientific advances with prevention messages that speak to young people.

The Phase 3 trial examined lenacapavir, an injectable HIV prevention drug administered twice a year. In its primary analysis, none of the 2,134 women who received the drug acquired HIV.

The results highlighted the potential of long-acting prevention, but Bekker argues that medical advances must be matched by communication that resonates with young people.

“Beating the old drum about the horrors of HIV, and shouting to youths about condoms is not necessarily going to cut it,” she said.

She believes prevention efforts need to move beyond fear-based messages and give young people accurate information, accessible services and the freedom to make informed decisions without judgement.

That task has become more difficult amid funding pressures. UNAIDS reported in March 2025 that disruptions to US-funded HIV programmes in Zimbabwe had affected services for key populations, including access to PrEP, testing and counselling.

Bekker has also raised concerns about whether prevention information reaches young people in ways they find relevant. Traditional pamphlets and warnings about abstinence or faithfulness may fail to engage those already making decisions about sex and relationships.

She argues that public health workers need to acknowledge young people’s realities and provide practical information about reducing risk, including through PrEP. Services must also be adolescent-friendly, allowing young people to ask questions and seek help without feeling judged.

In Harare, 23-year-old peer educator Angela Gutu is taking that message beyond the clinic.

Working with the Harare municipality, the health ministry, nongovernmental organisations and churches, she helps organise pop-up health services at markets, transport hubs, university campuses and sporting events. These are places young people already visit, bringing information and services closer to them rather than expecting them to navigate a formal health facility.

The distinction matters, Gutu says. For some young people, asking for an HIV test or screening for a sexually transmitted infection at a clinic can be intimidating. Fear of judgement or harsh treatment by health workers can discourage them from seeking help.

At the pop-up clinics, young people can access HIV self-testing kits and condoms, while mobile health workers provide referrals for PrEP and other services. Peer educators can help make those conversations less daunting, giving young people an opportunity to ask questions in an environment where they feel more comfortable.

“It’s about speaking young people’s lingo, taking away the HIV stigma,” Gutu said.

Her work reflects a growing recognition that making prevention services available is not enough. They must also be approachable, confidential and responsive to the concerns young people bring with them.

Zimbabwe’s health authorities say they are also working to bring prevention and treatment closer to communities.

Dr Innocent Hove, Provincial Medical Officer for Harare Metropolitan Province, told reporters, including Al Jazeera, at an August meeting that tackling HIV among young Zimbabweans was an urgent priority.

The government is decentralising services including PrEP, PEP, HIV testing and treatment, as well as screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections and tuberculosis.

Hove also pointed to mobile healthcare trucks being used to reach people in areas where conventional health facilities are difficult to access, including informal mining communities and remote artisanal gold-mining sites.

Such outreach could help people whose work, distance from clinics or financial circumstances make regular visits difficult. But its impact will depend on whether services are consistently available and reach those most in need.

For young people, access means more than knowing that PrEP or HIV testing exists. It means being able to obtain services without prohibitive costs, long journeys or fear of stigma.

Bongani, who plans to volunteer as a peer educator through the health ministry’s programme in January, wants to help make prevention information more accessible to his generation.

“My generation was born with the best array of HIV prevention tools. It’ll be a tragedy if AIDS deaths make a dramatic comeback due to our reckless behaviours,” he said.

articles.title: How Kent may have inspired George Orwell's Animal Farm
articles.summary: The county should be proud of its links to the famous author, a local historian tells the BBC.
articles.body:
Kent is well known for its literary connections.

Charles Dickens, Jane Austen, Ian Fleming, TS Eliot and HG Wells - to name just a few - all drew inspiration from the county in their works.

Lesser known is that George Orwell, author of Animal Farm and 1984, also had connections to the garden of England.

Local historian Terry Bird said he did not understand why this association had slipped under the radar.

"When you think of Kent's literary history, you [don't] think of... George Orwell," he told Secret Kent .

The author - under his real name of Eric Blair - is recorded as living at a chicken farm in Smarden in the 1921 census.

Bird said the reason he was there was unknown.

Whether Orwell was still at Eton - where he went to school - or if he had just left was "not quite clear", he added.

He next came to Kent in 1931, coming down from London and staying in West Malling Tramps Home for a night.

Orwell recorded his memories of this experience in a published essay.

Before moving on, he picked hops for a couple of weeks.

The historian pushed back on rumours that a Manor Farm near Wateringbury inspired the setting of Animal Farm - Orwell's allegorical take on the 1917 Russian Revolution, where farmyard animals kick out their human master only to face a new tyranny.

"Manor Farm is a very common name," Bird told the BBC. "It's a coincidence."

However, Bird said Manor Farm was instead inspired by Brewers Hall Farm in Mereworth, where Orwell picked hops.

He added it was owned by the Blest family, who had an "extensive network" of hop farms across the county.

"At the time, the villages around here were swamped by hop pickers - more numerous than the local inhabitants," said Bird.

Orwell was accommodated in a tin hut, one form of temporary accommodation used to house the workers, he said.

Other locations have also been pointed to as inspiration for Manor Farm.

Some claim it is based on Chalk Farm in Willingdon, near Eastbourne where the author went to school as a child.

Old Major - the wise old boar that inspires the animal rebellion - is referred to as Willingdon Beauty.

A farm in Hertfordshire has similarly been cited as an inspiration for the book.

Orwell's next appearance in Kent was a stay in Preston Hall Hospital for around six months between 1938 and 1939.

Bird explained that the author, who had a history of chest illness, had begun coughing up blood that year.

His wife's brother was a well-known consultant for chest problems and sent him to the hospital, which had been established for soldiers returning from World War One with tuberculosis.

"He improved a bit while he was there," said Bird. "He had very good treatment."

Kent should be proud of its Orwell links, he added.

articles.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
articles.summary: Both Hamas and IDF officials confirm the death of Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade.
articles.body:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".

It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".

Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.

He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.

Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued occasional strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.

articles.title: Women with autoimmune diseases often misdiagnosed for 4 years or more
articles.summary: Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.”
articles.body: Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.” An online survey by British researchers found that it took women with an autoimmune disorder about four years to get a diagnosis, while it took men around three months to less than a year. It adds to previous research showing disparities in diagnosis between men and women with autoimmune disorders. “Women in particular felt not listened to or not heard or not believed by their medical professionals,” said Sydnae Taylor, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oxford in the U.K. and co-author of the study published recently in eClinicalMedicine. Autoimmune diseases — including Type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis — occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body. More than 23 million people in the U.S. have an autoimmune disease, and most of them are women. Autoimmune thyroid disease, which includes Hashimoto’s, was the most common type reported by women in the survey. It typically causes fatigue, unexplained weight gain and sensitivity to cold, among other symptoms. Autoimmune conditions can affect anyone but are more common in women than in men, according to the federal Office on Women’s Health. For example, around 90% of people with lupus are women, according to the Lupus Foundation of America. It’s not clear why women are more at risk. Research from the Mayo Clinic has suggested differences in the microbiome, sex hormones and that women’s bodies produce higher levels of antibodies that are associated with autoimmune disorders. A 2024 Stanford Medicine study found clues in a molecule connected to the X chromosome. Because many of the disorders share similar symptoms in the early stages — fatigue, dizziness, low-grade fever, as well as stress, anxiety and depression — they can be difficult to diagnose. Women and men have similar symptoms, but with women specifically, “they develop over time, so it’s often hard to recognize right at the beginning,” said Dr. Saira Z. Sheikh, the director of the UNC Rheumatology Lupus Clinic in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Symptoms can appear during childhood and last throughout adulthood. The survey was conducted through social media, patient support groups and community groups of underserved populations such as religious groups and the homeless population. It was translated into five languages as a way to reach diverse communities. Participants shared data about symptom onset, how many clinicians were consulted and misdiagnosis. The data was then compared between men and women. Out of the 6,607 participants, 91.2% were women and the majority of them were from the United Kingdom. Misdiagnosis is more likely when symptoms are “invisible,” meaning they aren’t detected in a blood test or involve pain, fatigue and neurological symptoms such as tingling, Taylor said. In these situations, accurate diagnoses rely on doctors listening and believing the patient. “We shouldn’t assume that women’s symptoms are psychological simply because the initial investigations are inconclusive,” Sheikh said.

articles.title: Simple salt substitute could prevent three million deaths a year worldwide, study estimates
articles.summary: A Nature Health study finds potassium salt substitutes could prevent nearly 3 million deaths yearly, but hyperkalemia poses risks for some patients.
articles.body: Replacing regular table salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths and more than 10 million cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide every year, according to a major study published in Nature Health. Researchers at the Australia-based George Institute for Global Health analyzed dietary patterns and disease risks among 4.6 billion adults across 193 countries to estimate the potential benefits of the switch. The study relied on mathematical simulations rather than a clinical trial, using estimates that can vary in accuracy, the researchers acknowledged. HIGH SALT INTAKE LINKED TO FASTER MEMORY DECLINE IN ONE GROUP, STUDY FINDS High blood pressure affects roughly 1.4 billion adults worldwide and is a leading cause of strokes, heart attacks and chronic kidney damage, according to the World Health Organization. Consuming too much salt can contribute to high blood pressure, as its sodium content causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and putting added pressure on artery walls. Potassium-enriched salt replaces some sodium with potassium while looking, tasting and cooking like regular salt. The swap reduces sodium intake while boosting potassium, which helps relax blood vessels and promotes the removal of excess sodium from the body, according to the researchers. If households replaced only the salt used in home cooking and at the dining table, the model projected 1.85 million fewer deaths and 6.19 million fewer new cases of heart and kidney disease annually. ANCIENT CHINESE MOVEMENT SHOWS PROMISE FOR REDUCING BLOOD PRESSURE AT HOME, STUDY SAYS In another scenario, replacing salt only in restaurant meals and processed foods was projected to prevent about 1.56 million deaths and 5.46 million new disease cases annually. In a more targeted scenario, researchers projected that switching 80% of adults with diagnosed high blood pressure to potassium-enriched household salt could prevent about 590,000 deaths worldwide each year. The projected benefits varied by region, depending on population size and sources of dietary sodium. The largest potential benefit was seen in China, with an estimated 1.08 million deaths averted each year under full replacement. India followed with nearly 400,000 preventable deaths, while the U.S. could potentially avoid roughly 105,000 deaths and 492,000 new disease cases annually. POPULAR FOOD COULD BOOST HEART HEALTH, BUT THE AMOUNT YOU NEED TO EAT MAY SURPRISE YOU In many Asian and African countries, most dietary salt comes from home cooking, suggesting that greater awareness and access to potassium-enriched alternatives could encourage healthier habits, according to the researchers. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Broader adoption by food manufacturers and restaurants would be needed to maximize the health benefits in Western countries, where more than 70% of dietary sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods, the study suggested. "This study shows that small changes have an enormous impact on two prominent diseases globally: cardiovascular disease and kidney disease," Dr. Nathan Goodyear of the Williams Cancer Institute in California told Fox News Digital. Goodyear, who was not involved in the study, said the bigger take-home message is that health is "not something that we’re just born with." "It’s something that we cultivate. It’s the environment we cultivate," he said. "And this environment influences the potential for disease harvest long before disease is diagnosed." Potential risks While the study's models suggested that the heart health benefits outweighed the risks for the overall population, experts cautioned that the substitute may not be safe for everyone. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Potassium-enriched salt substitutes can also pose risks, including hyperkalemia, a condition in which excess potassium builds up in the blood and can trigger dangerous irregular heart rhythms, according to the National Kidney Foundation. The body normally removes excess potassium through urine, but people with advanced kidney disease or those taking certain blood pressure medications may have difficulty eliminating it. The World Health Organization advises against potassium-enriched salt substitutes for people with kidney problems that impair potassium removal, unless recommended by a healthcare professional. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "We’re constantly in medicine looking for the magic bullet in causation, magic bullet in disease treatment, [but] that does not exist," said Goodyear. Widespread adoption could also face challenges, as potassium-enriched salt costs about twice as much as regular salt on average and would require cooperation from food manufacturers and suppliers, according to the researchers.

articles.title: AI mosquito trap targets deadly dengue outbreak
articles.summary: USF researchers built an AI mosquito trap with over 98% accuracy as Florida battles its largest dengue outbreak in decades with 524 local cases.
articles.body: You probably aren't thinking much about mosquitoes in November. In much of the country, cooler weather has sent those annoying little bloodsuckers into hiding. But in Florida, mosquitoes are still causing serious trouble. The state is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades, and hundreds of people have caught the virus without leaving the state. Now, researchers at the University of South Florida have developed an AI mosquito trap that could help health officials find dangerous mosquito species much faster. It can identify mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. And with dengue still spreading in Florida, the timing couldn't be more important. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE Why Florida's dengue outbreak is making headlines now If you thought mosquito season ended when summer did, Florida has a different story to tell. According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County has recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, the county's largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, health officials have reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. That means people contracted the virus from mosquitoes in the area rather than while traveling overseas. The Tampa area has been hit especially hard. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain. In serious cases, it can lead to life-threatening complications. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. On November 13, Hillsborough County announced that it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments to help contain the outbreak. County officials say mosquito surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area. And here's why we're talking about this in November. While mosquitoes have largely disappeared from colder parts of the country, they can remain active in warmer states. Florida's outbreak shows that the threat doesn't disappear simply because summer is over. Meanwhile, a new generation of technology could give communities a better way to respond before mosquito populations get out of control. How the new AI mosquito trap works The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by researchers at the University of South Florida. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have been developing the system through research dating back to 2018. Their goal is to help mosquito control teams identify the insects they're catching without spending days examining them under a microscope. The trap itself looks fairly straightforward. Workers can hang it from a low tree branch or place it on the ground. A light or bait attracts mosquitoes, and a small fan pulls them inside. Once the insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. Artificial intelligence then compares those images against a large database to determine which mosquito species have been captured. But the technology goes further. It can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. That's useful information because female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. The researchers say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing. GOOGLE WANTS TO RELEASE MILLIONS OF MOSQUITOES Why identifying mosquitoes faster could save lives Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. That's valuable work, but when health officials are trying to track a disease outbreak, waiting several days can slow their response. Digitomy wants to shorten that process dramatically. Its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured mosquito species the same day. That could help mosquito control teams see where potentially dangerous species are appearing and decide where to concentrate their efforts. This is especially important with Aedes aegypti, the mosquito species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases. Knowing which ones are present can help officials make better decisions. There's one important point to understand. The trap identifies mosquito species capable of carrying disease. It does not automatically prove that a captured mosquito is infected with dengue. Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus. AI mosquito traps could create an early warning system What I find particularly interesting is what happens after the trap identifies a mosquito. Digitomy can send that information to a mapping dashboard, allowing mosquito control teams to see where certain species are appearing. The goal is to give mosquito control teams access to that information the same day, helping them identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. Think about how useful that could be during an outbreak. If several traps begin detecting more Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in one neighborhood, officials could investigate that area and consider targeted mosquito control measures. Instead of waiting for more people to become sick, they could use surveillance data to guide their response. The researchers have already integrated trap information into a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard at mosquitodashboard.org/. That system also incorporates more than half a million citizen science reports. The idea is to combine information from automated traps with observations from people who help track mosquitoes. Digitomy's technology could also complement an existing early warning system developed by Carney for dengue and West Nile virus. Together, these tools could give public health departments a clearer view of mosquito activity across communities. Of course, detecting mosquitoes early doesn't guarantee that an outbreak can be prevented. But faster information could help officials respond sooner, particularly in areas where mosquito control resources are limited. When could communities start using these smart traps? Digitomy has already tested its technology at the University of South Florida and worked with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. The researchers are also preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County, where Florida's dengue outbreak has been especially severe. The startup is working with USF's Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito trap manufacturers. That could allow companies to add the technology to equipment they already produce. Digitomy is working toward commercial availability by licensing its AI technology to established mosquito trap manufacturers. For now, the university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. The company also received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation's Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026. The funding is intended to help accelerate the licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online education platform that would allow mosquito control professionals and the public to practice identifying mosquito species using images and AI-generated feedback. THIRD PERSON DIES AFTER MOSQUITO IS REPORTEDLY TRAPPED ON PLANE TO GERMANY IN 'AIRPORT MALARIA' PHENOMENON What this AI mosquito trap means for you You probably won't be hanging a Digitomy trap in your backyard anytime soon. But that doesn't mean this technology couldn't eventually affect your community. If mosquito control departments adopt smarter surveillance systems, they may be able to identify dangerous mosquito populations sooner and make better decisions about where to intervene. And even though we're heading into November, people living in warmer areas still need to pay attention to mosquito activity. If you're traveling to Florida or another place where mosquitoes remain active, taking precautions is important. For now, the best protection is still fairly simple. Empty standing water from flowerpots and other outdoor containers because mosquitoes can breed in surprisingly small amounts of water. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent when spending time outdoors. Wearing long sleeves and pants can also help reduce exposed skin. We've covered some useful products that can help keep mosquitoes away, including repellents and outdoor gadgets. You can find them in our guide to mosquito and tick repellents at CyberGuy.com Kurt's key takeaways I think this is one of those uses of AI that could make a real difference in people's lives. Most of us see mosquitoes as an annoying part of summer. But Florida's dengue outbreak is a reminder that these tiny insects can cause serious health problems, even late in the year. What interests me about Digitomy is the possibility of giving mosquito control teams information while they still have time to act. The technology looks promising, especially with its reported accuracy in laboratory testing. But I want to see how it performs in real-world conditions before calling it a breakthrough. If it works as researchers hope, communities could have a valuable new tool to help protect people from mosquito-borne diseases. And that's a use of AI I can get behind. articles.title: Classic American pantry staples are getting a major protein- and fiber-packed makeover
articles.summary: Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane says brands were underinvested for over a decade as the company unveils protein Jell-O and cheesy ramen cups.
articles.body: Cheesy ramen, protein-packed Jell-O and round bacon slices specially cut for sandwiches are among the new twists coming to grocery stores as Kraft Heinz reportedly tries to breathe new life into old brands. The new products, expected to hit shelves in the spring, are part of a broader push by the packaged-food giant to invest in innovation. They include Jell-O pudding with 10 grams of protein, Crystal Light with added fiber and protein, and Oscar Mayer Sandwich Bacon. "It’s a big turnaround," Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane told the Wall Street Journal. "These brands have been underinvested in for over 10 years." CAMPBELL'S ROLLS OUT NEW SOUPS, INCLUDING FIRST-EVER GLUTEN-FREE CHICKEN NOODLE VARIETY Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen is set to arrive nationwide in early 2027, according to a press release. The instant noodle cups will come in Spicy, Chicken and Pork varieties and contain no artificial flavors, preservatives or dyes. Kraft said it is the brand’s first move into a new category in nearly 20 years and Cahillane said it sold out within a week of its Canadian launch. The launch also follows the brand’s introduction of PowerMac, mac and cheese with added protein and fiber. Cahillane told the Journal that PowerMac helped return the brand to sales growth after several years. AMERICA'S FAVORITE PIZZA MAY BE GETTING A MAKEOVER AS PROTEIN DEMAND SURGES Kraft Heinz has invested an additional $700 million in its business, with funding for marketing, lower prices, staffing and product development. It also hired 400 employees, the outlet reported. Its new offerings reflect consumers’ growing interest in protein and wellness, but the company is also staying true to its roots, focusing on taste and convenience. WENDY'S BETS ON THICKER BACON, CREAMIER FROSTY IN BID TO REVERSE SALES SLUMP About half of its 2027 product pipeline will focus on health and wellness, Cahillane told the Journal, including products with less sugar or more protein. But traditional Heinz ketchup will still be made with high-fructose corn syrup, he said, in part because cane sugar is more expensive. "We’re not trying to claim that 100% of our portfolio is grown in your back garden," Cahillane said. "We are claiming that we can do health and wellness. We can play in that space, and we can do it extremely well." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Oscar Mayer meat and Kraft cheese continue to struggle, according to Cahillane, as is Philadelphia cream cheese with consumers switching to cottage cheese. Kraft Heinz is trying to develop cream cheese products that rely less on carbohydrates like bagels. Kraft Heinz at one point planned to split into two companies, separating its global condiments business from its North American grocery unit, but Cahillane later paused the plan, telling the Journal that a split is no longer a focus. But some analysts remain skeptical that the company’s struggling brands can be revived.
