articles.title: Common blood pressure drug helps more stroke survivors reach critical health target
articles.summary: The REDUCE trial found spironolactone lowered blood pressure by nearly eight points in stroke survivors, but key questions about prevention remain.
articles.body: A low-cost medication could help stroke survivors whose blood pressure remains elevated despite treatment, a new study suggests. The research, known as the REDUCE trial, looked at whether adding spironolactone, a medication commonly known as a water pill, could help lower blood pressure after a stroke. The findings were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, Nov. 6-9, 2026, in Chicago. Participants were split into two groups. One added spironolactone to their regular treatment, while the other continued with usual post-stroke care. SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE Researchers tracked the participants' blood pressure at home over the following six months to determine whether adding the medication made a difference. After three months, the top blood pressure number was nearly eight points lower on average among people taking spironolactone compared with those receiving usual care – about 126 versus 133, the study said. More patients taking spironolactone also reached the recommended blood pressure goal of less than 130/80. That included 52% of those taking the medication compared with 30% receiving usual care. "Lowering blood pressure is the most important step in preventing another stroke, yet many survivors struggle to reach recommended blood pressure targets after a stroke," study co-lead author Dr. Jordana Cohen, an associate professor of medicine and epidemiology at the University of Pennsylvania, said in a news release. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "When spironolactone was added to post-stroke care, we saw a meaningful drop in blood pressure that may lower the risk of future strokes and heart attacks," she added. Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency physician and former chief medical officer who was not involved in the research, said the findings are encouraging, but do not yet show that the medication prevents a subsequent stroke. "We already know that controlling blood pressure lowers the risk of another stroke," Joshua told Fox News Digital. "This study measured blood pressure, so whether adding spironolactone leads to fewer repeat strokes is still an open question." Spironolactone works by helping the body get rid of extra salt and water, which can lower blood pressure, according to the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It also causes the body to hold onto potassium, so patients taking it need to have their levels checked, the drug’s prescribing information states. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Joshua warned that high potassium is one of the main safety concerns because it can develop without symptoms. The risk can be higher for people with kidney problems and those taking certain medications or potassium supplements. The medication can also lower blood pressure enough to cause dizziness, he added. "If your blood pressure is still high after a stroke, bring your home readings to your clinician and ask whether this medication is a good fit," Joshua advised. Study limitations The trial ended early with 160 participants instead of the planned 200, and about 15% did not have blood pressure readings available at the three-month mark, the researchers noted. People taking spironolactone were also taking slightly more blood pressure medications overall than those receiving usual care. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The study was not designed to determine whether spironolactone actually prevents another stroke or heart attack. Larger and longer studies are needed to answer that question, according to the researchers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

articles.title: Woman’s kratom addiction spiraled from 4 capsules to 100 a day: ‘Zombie shell of myself’
articles.summary: Hilary Tesluck shares how kratom capsules led to a spiraling addiction, with her daily intake climbing to 100 capsules before she sought help.
articles.body: Kratom-related reports to U.S. poison centers rose about 1,200% from 2015 to 2025, reaching a record high of 3,434 last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For Hilary Tesluck, a 30-year-old woman in Michigan, the potential for addiction began well before those numbers emerged. Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21. KRATOM INDUSTRY WARNS SYNTHETIC OPIOIDS SHOULD NOT BE CALLED 'KRATOM' Her initial use involved leaf kratom rather than concentrated 7-OH products, she shared. The American Kratom Association argues that 7-OH should be distinguished from natural leaf kratom, while acknowledging that kratom itself can cause dependence. "It was introduced to me by a friend who knew that I was someone who suffered from anxiety and took prescription medication for it," Tesluck told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be more holistic and natural in what I was consuming." She noted that she doesn’t recall any dosing recommendations on the label. "I didn’t know how much to take, but my friend told me to take four capsules." WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS At first, Tesluck – an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring – noticed the substance gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity. Growing dependence Tesluck's daily intake climbed gradually. "Very slowly, over time, I had to take just one more capsule or just one more dose, and then went all the way up to 100," she said. Her day-to-day functioning began to suffer, she shared. "I was not doing very well at work. I was getting … written up for performance." Physically, she had lost nearly 40 pounds and struggled to even stand in the shower "because my body was so wasted away." Tesluck’s belief that kratom was natural and legal made her growing dependence difficult to accept, she said. "About a year and a half into my kratom addiction from just the leaf … I finally realized I needed to do something, and I needed help." Seeking help When she first sought treatment in 2020, Tesluck described feeling dismissed, saying that the facility’s urine test did not detect her use and that she had to explain what kratom was to the staff. "They were confused why I was there," she said. "So I left after just a few days because I felt kind of humiliated, and I went right back to my use." Tesluck found more help in 2021, when she attended an online recovery meeting. "I had nothing to lose," she said. "It changed everything for me to hear other people telling my story for the first time." After years of feeling alone in her addiction, she said, she finally felt surrounded by people who understood. "It’s one problem at two strengths." In 2023, Tesluck relapsed following her grandmother’s death. "I was just grief-stricken. She was really close to me," she said. "So I went to the smoke shop just to get a little bit of kratom, just one time." She later experienced a separate relapse involving 7-OH, which she said followed the death of her cat and the end of a relationship on the same night. MEN AND WOMEN WHO SMOKE MARIJUANA MAY EXPERIENCE DIFFERENT EFFECTS, STUDY SUGGESTS 7-OH, short for 7-hydroxymitragynine, occurs naturally in trace amounts in kratom. Concentrated 7-OH products contain much higher levels than the leaf itself. The body converts some of kratom’s main active compound, mitragynine, into 7-OH, research shows. Both compounds act on opioid receptors and can contribute to dependence, according to the FDA. "The 7-OH was very strong," Tesluck said. "I stayed on that for just a few months because of how intense it was." She returned to her recovery group for support. "I had to take a leave of absence, and I got clean from 7-OH again with their help," she said. Having struggled with both leaf kratom and 7-OH, Tesluck views them as closely connected. "It’s one problem at two strengths," she said. ‘SUPER-DRUG’ 10 TIMES STRONGER THAN FENTANYL LINKED TO DEATHS ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association, disputed this characterization of leaf kratom and concentrated 7-OH. In comments to Fox News Digital, he argued that the body’s conversion of mitragynine into 7-OH does not produce equivalent exposure to concentrated products. Haddow also raised the possibility that the capsules Tesluck initially consumed may have contained ingredients beyond natural leaf kratom. Varying regulations Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans. "It’s really been a patchwork," Tesluck said. "It’s different from state to state. Some states ban it, some states regulate it." Florida, for example, prohibits selling or providing kratom products to anyone under 21. Washington’s health department says unscheduled kratom products remain largely unregulated there, without age restrictions, labeling standards or ingredient-testing requirements. Texas law requires kratom product labels to include directions and a recommended serving size. "We support stronger enforcement across the board." Haddow also emphasized the need for consumer warnings, adding, "The American Kratom Association supports accurate labeling to warn consumers that kratom can cause dependence." "We support stronger enforcement across the board, and excise taxes on kratom products to fund that enforcement." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER In an October interview with Fox News Digital, Haddow also backed age restrictions. "Twenty-one and up should be the only people who have access to these products," he said. Tesluck also raised concerns about how the products are marketed, describing social media ads as looking "very harmless" or "very cool," potentially drawing consumers’ interest. "It’s something that you might want to try just based on the marketing itself and the packaging," she warned. Tesluck said her work regularly brings her into contact with parents grieving children whose deaths they attribute to kratom products, including in states with Kratom Consumer Protection Acts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The FDA says no kratom drugs are approved by the agency, and that kratom cannot legally be marketed as a dietary supplement or added to conventional foods. In December 2025, federal authorities seized approximately 73,000 concentrated 7-OH products valued at roughly $1 million from three Missouri firms, according to the FDA. Warning signs People taking kratom should pay attention to whether their use is beginning to dictate their daily routines, including planning around obtaining it or worrying about running out, Tesluck urged. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Like making sure when the smoke shop closes that you have enough time to get there," she said. Diminished appetite, weight loss and hair loss were among the effects Tesluck experienced. Other signs of problematic kratom use may include cravings, higher consumption than intended, unsuccessful attempts to stop and continued use despite problems at work or home, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Feeling unable to miss a dose was another concern for Tesluck. "If I took less than what I was taking, I would feel even worse and sicker," she recalled. "So I was kind of stuck at that baseline with kratom." Haddow acknowledged that consumers can develop dependence or addiction. "I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall." "Kratom can cause physical dependence, and some consumers have reported they develop addiction to kratom," he told Fox News Digital. Feelings of sedation, numbness or irritability may also occur, Tesluck said. "I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall," she said. "I wasn’t really the same person, personality-wise. I was irritable. I was mean." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." She serves as executive director of End Kratom Addiction, a Virginia-based nonprofit that aims to raise awareness of kratom-related risks and advocates for stronger regulation. "My advocacy looks a lot like meeting one-on-one with families … and coordinating resources for those who are still in addiction," she said.

articles.title: Here’s Exactly How Often to Eat Leafy Greens to Support Brain Health, According to a Dietitian
articles.summary: Dark, leafy greens are some of the best foods to support your long-term brain health. Here’s how often to eat them for those benefits, dietitian says.
articles.body: What you put on your plate can boost your health, including your brain health. But to actually get those benefits, you may need to eat more than you think. “We know that our bodies thrive when we eat well, and so does our brain,” said registered dietitian Joy Bauer on a Nov. 4 segment of the TODAY Show. And it’s probably no surprise that dark, leafy greens are among Bauer’s best foods for brain health. If you want to eat more of these tasty, nutritious foods to support your noggin, here’s exactly how much you should add to your plate each day. Expert Tip of the Day: Eat Leafy Greens Regularly for Brain Health Benefits According to research, you should aim to eat 1 to 2 cups of dark, leafy greens every day to reap their brain-health benefits, Bauer said. “I know it sounds like a lot, but that is what the research is based on,” she explained. “Your brain is going to thank you.” Why It Matters “Studies do show there is a correlation between what we put on our plate and how we remember and how we think and remember,” Bauer explained. “So every single bite is a chance to really feed your brain.” Dark, leafy greens are among the most beneficial foods you can eat for brain health. Bauer specifically made a point give a “shoutout to kale and spinach,” she said, “because they have folate, a B vitamin that’s linked to memory.” You’ll also find a compound called lutein in these greens, which is an antioxidant that supports eye and brain function. Other dark, leafy greens include arugula, bok choy, watercress, mustard greens, collard and chard. And keep in mind that green, leafy vegetables like broccoli and Brussels sprouts count too. How to Get Started The most obvious way to eat a cup or two of leafy greens is in a salad. Try adding some other brain-boosting foods, including beans, hard-boiled eggs or grilled salmon. You could also sneak your greens into other foods by blending them into a vibrant pasta sauce, smoothies, scrambled eggs or a quiche. Bauer’s other top brain foods include: BerriesFishEggsBeans Nuts and seeds, especially walnuts and chia seeds, also provide anti-inflammatory compounds that support your brain health in addition to a dose of filling plant-based protein. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Jailed Pakistan ex-PM Imran Khan writes to judges, seeks vital medical care
articles.summary: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party founder says court orders on his care were ignored and he ‘may not return alive’.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan’s top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, in an open letter released by his lawyer.

Lawyer Salman Safdar posted the letter on X on Monday, describing it as a “humanitarian plea for medical treatment”. It is Khan’s first such letter since he fell ill earlier this year.

Safdar said Khan gave him instructions and notes during a three-hour meeting at Central Jail Rawalpindi, also known as Adiala Jail, on November 11, and that he prepared the letter solely on that basis.

Khan, 74, has been in jail since August 2023, following convictions that his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), says are politically motivated.

In the letter, he said he had been held in solitary confinement “for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025, when he and Bushra Bibi were sentenced to 17 years in one of several cases against them.

He said he had lost 85 percent of the vision in his right eye and that doctors had told him he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

Khan wrote that he had “never once sought relief on medical grounds, nor used illness as a tactic”.

“I fought on the merits, with confidence, and I still do,” he said. “I do not ask Your Lordships for any favour.”

On August 18, the Supreme Court ordered that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and examined by a medical board. “That order has not been implemented,” he wrote.

Instead, he was taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) and returned to jail within hours.

Khan was taken to hospital again late on November 10 for an eye injection. PIMS said he was “clinically stable”, while Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said he was receiving the required care.

Khan also raised concerns about Bushra Bibi, whom he married in 2018. He said she suffered a retinal detachment in April and underwent “complicated eye surgery in secrecy”.

Without another operation, he said, “she may lose her sight permanently”.

Her lawyers filed an application at the Islamabad High Court on Monday seeking her complete medical record and immediate transfer to a specialised hospital.

Two of Khan’s sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were released from a Lahore jail on November 12 after nearly two months in detention. Aleema Khan, a third sister, remains in jail, according to PTI.

The government said it detained the sisters over a possible threat to law and order in advance of PTI’s Islamabad march planned for September 27, which did not go ahead.

Sayed Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader, said ex-PM Khan had been left with no other option but to seek further legal intervention.

“He’s been left with no choice but to write this open letter because, over three years of imprisonment and solitary confinement, he has seen that justice has only been seen in small flashes and then gone away,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera.

Bukhari said the letter did not mean Khan was giving up.

“He is asking for no favours. He is asking for no deal. He is asking for justice and the legal system of Pakistan to work,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera. “All it shows is a man humbly asking for justice and humane medical treatment.”

Bukhari said the party wanted the courts to press the government to act.

“We want the courts to hear his proceedings adequately … rather than adjourning and postponing them,” he said. “And we want the courts to apply enough pressure on the government that real medical treatment should be provided so that there is no loss of life, no loss of vision.”

Mehmal Sarfraz, a Lahore-based political analyst, said the letter reflected Khan’s concern about his wife’s health.

“He is very worried about his wife’s deteriorating health and is looking for relief for her,” Sarfraz told Al Jazeera.

Another Lahore-based political analyst, Habib Akram, said he did not see the letter as a plea for mercy.

“If he were asking for mercy, he would not have needed to write this letter. He has written to the courts, not to anyone else,” Akram told Al Jazeera. “And what is he asking for? He is asking for his rights, which he has cited from the jail manual.”

Akram, however, was sceptical that the letter would change Khan’s circumstances.

“What is being done to Imran Khan has lost its legal grounds. The Islamabad High Court has an order that he can meet visitors on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The Supreme Court has also ruled. Neither was followed, but a third order was suddenly complied with,” he said.

“This is no longer a legal issue. I don’t think the Supreme Court’s order will be implemented because of this letter.”
